title: 14 years on, the creator of DayZ is still searching for a solution to survival gaming's biggest problem: 'I think I am going to die without having solved it'
text:
You might think making one of the most influential games of this century would be a source of unending happiness for its creator. But for Dean 'Rocket' Hall, founder of RocketWerkz, the relationship with his most famous creation isn't that simple. "When DayZ happened, it was like dying," says Hall of the mod which, alongside Minecraft, helped establish survival games as a cornerstone of the medium. "It ended my old life. My relationship with everyone who I knew up to that point changed completely."
This isn't to say Hall doesn't recognise his good fortune: "It was obviously an amazing thing that happened to me," he stresses. But there is a sense that, while Hall gained much from the creation of DayZ—fame, respect, and to a certain extent, fortune—something was lost too. "I loved making the mod, and I loved that feeling, and I've been chasing it ever since."
(Image credit: Bohemia Interactive) Chasing the feeling of making DayZ has taken over a decade, sent Hall down numerous rabbit holes and even led his studio to the precipice of bankruptcy. After all that time, Hall still hasn't found what he is looking for and admits he may never find it. Yet as he continues his search, RocketWerkz is beginning to find success on its own terms.
Hall of fame
What is it, exactly, that would rekindle the feeling of making DayZ for Hall? Specifically, he says he's searching for a solution to a specific problem he sees in survival games. "You see it time [and] again. If you go see commentary on a survival game, people will say it gets boring, or the end game sucks," he says. "And it's such a hard problem, because what you do [to] solve it [is] brute force it with heaps of content."
It's not clear when exactly Hall identified this issue, but it was likely between RocketWerkz's first and second released games. When the DayZ mod launched, Hall was working at Bohemia Interactive, the creators of ArmA 2 which served as the original basis for DayZ.
This wasn't the first mod Hall had made for ArmA 2. Indeed, it was modding that landed Hall his job at Bohemia, after his co-op mod for ArmA 2 became the most popular mod on the defunct ArmA fansite Armaholic. Despite running a major video game developer, Hall still regularly makes mods today for games like RimWorld and Barotrauma .
"People think I'm a game developer who came up from [being] a modder, and I would say I'm a modder who makes games during the day," Hall explains. "I was born a modder and I will die a modder. And I think if there's a lesson out there for any aspiring game devs, I think it's mod games. You will learn even faster than making them."
DayZ's surging popularity led Bohemia Interactive to begin creating a commercial version of the mod. Hall initially led the project, but he left Bohemia in 2014, which is when he founded RocketWerkz and began work on a project called Ion.
Ion would later be cancelled, with RocketWerkz pivoting to Stationeers , a space-station construction and management game inspired by one of Hall's favourite games, Space Station 13. Yet when it was released in 2017, Stationeers received mixed reviews, and has struggled commercially throughout its existence. "It's built up about seven years of losses," Hall says, though he adds that in 2025 it "actually probably broke even."
Close to the sun
While well received by players, Stationeers struggled commercially and remains in Steam early access. Following Stationeers, RocketWerkz began developing Icarus , a free-to-play, online survival game with a run-based loop. Players would land on a planet, go through the basic survival loop while completing an objective, launch back into space, and begin another mission that would start the cycle again.
(Image credit: RocketWerkz) This was Hall's attempt to solve that problem of survival games running out of road. But there were two problems. First, players didn't like the loop, as they perceived it as losing progress. "It just didn't work. People didn't want it. It was hilarious, but that's life."
Second, on launch, Icarus was not the financial success that RocketWerkz needed it to be to survive. As such, RocketWerkz pivoted quickly, abandoning the free-to-play aspect and committing to a rigorous post-launch support scheme where it would release weekly updates like clockwork. "After the beta weekend, I levelled with the team. I was like 'We do this or it's over.' We might even do all this work and still go bankrupt, " he says. Hall is open about how gruelling a process this was. "The last couple of years, I've been enjoying it, but before that, I hated it, and we were looking at ruin, basically."
Nonetheless, Icarus has slowly established a trusting audience, one which RocketWerkz could then sell larger, paid expansions to. "Icarus, at times, we can have a 50% attachment rate to DLC at purchase," Hall explains. "I can tell you right now, the studio would be bankrupt if we didn't do that strategy."
(Image credit: Rocketwerkz) Yet even here, the margins can be slim. "People will go and say: 'There's too many DLC, this is crazy'. And I'll post our financials. I'll be like 'Hey, a lot of our DLC, even on Icarus— which is really good—sometimes we'll only make $100,000 from it. It might have cost us $120,000 to make. So we're not printing money."
Indeed, Hall says that it's only in the last year that Icarus has really begun making money. "We've increased our revenue 80% in the last year," he says. "Our dream for a long time has been to make more per day than we spend, because as a game developer, you need to build a big cash reserve, especially now because there's no investment money out there."
Rocket purr-kz
The experience of making Icarus has taught Hall a lot. He says he's learned the value of community, how a relatively small audience can be more valuable than hundreds of thousands of players—provided the audience is dedicated enough. "My encouragement to devs is: focus on getting fans, not on selling product."
He also believes a small audience can be just as emotionally gratifying as a large one. "I think seeing that 100 people love what you do is chemically the same as 100,000 at least," Hall elaborates. "If you're a musician [like] Freddie Mercury and you pack out the Wembley Stadium, seeing 100,000 people right there waving lighters is probably insane. But as a Game Dev, I don't know whether there's as big a difference. So if I can make a mod that 100 people love, that's like crack cocaine to me."
(Image credit: RocketWerkz) It was this line of thinking that informed RocketWerkz' approach with Kitten Space Agency —the studio's freely available spiritual successor to Kerbal Space Program, a game which Hall personally adores. "With Kitten Space Agency, the game is completely free. It's funded entirely by contributions. So that really puts it in front of the gamer's face," he says. "If you want this game to exist, how much is it worth? Because it's all on you."
While letting players determine the value of a game has its own risks, Hall likes it as a funding model, saying it absolves him of the need to justify a price point, and allows him to focus on the creative aspect: "I think if I could, I would just do all my games for free, because it stops you having to be focused on dumb stuff, and allows you to focus on the good stuff, which is what you get to do for modding."
Beyond survival
One thing Hall is still yet to learn, however, is how to solve his perceived problem with survival games. Icarus ended up using the exact brute-forcing solution he wanted to avoid. "Make no mistake, that's all we ended up doing with Icarus. It's such a crude, basic way to make your game, is just to solve it with content, I am really proud of what we've done with that. But it's like banging a nail in with a rock."
What is the solution, then? One idea Hall has identified is "to layer pressures in that hit you at different points." He cites Valheim as an example. "It does it with these boss fights. And the fun part of the boss fights in Valheim is not the boss fights, it's preparing for the boss fights."
(Image credit: RocketWerkz) Another example Hall points to is EnviroMine, a mod for Minecraft that adds an insanity meter to the experience. "The more time you spent underground, you built up this insanity meter, and it was this weird extra pressure that I'd never considered, that just totally changed how you played the game," Hall explains. "It was one of those mechanics that made me go 'Oh, I wish I'd come up with that'".
Both examples suggest that survival games need to aspire to a higher level of experience to become self-sustaining. But Hall doesn't think either have landed on the perfect solution. In fact, he's not sure if anyone ever will, and that includes himself. "I think I am going to die without having solved it," he says.
But this won't stop Hall from trying. Now that RocketWerkz is solvent, he's putting every penny it earns into the pot for its next project—which he's described as a DayZ/ArmA style game. "I've never made any money from RocketWerkz. All the money goes back in," he says. "Our aim was to try to build money so we could make a big game, and that's really hard."

title: Elden Ring's Tarnished Edition is exciting enough on its own, but it's also our last chance to properly experience the game's launch day hype
text:
Play This Right Now
Welcome to Play This Right Now, the site version of our weekly newsletter in which we celebrate a new game, update, or DLC that we think is well worth checking out. You can subscribe to the newsletter at the link if you want to get our thoughts about a new videogame happening direct to your inbox every Thursday.
Elden Ring is one of the best videogames I've ever played, and now, four years from launch, is possibly the last time you'll get to experience it as an event . The Tarnished Edition DLC looks small on paper⁠—two new classes and a smattering of armor and items⁠—but it is still something new, something unexpected added to our 2022 game of the year.
What in any other context might make for a Horse Armor -style embarrassment is one of the most exciting releases of 2026 for me, and I'm only, like, a quarter joking. Elden Ring is the type of game that made a couple borked quests getting patched into a massive communal treasure hunt . New weapons, armor, and classes at this late date feels like a profound gift, even if I'm paying for the privilege.
But, in addition to the material additions coming to Elden Ring, the Tarnished Edition DLC serves as an enticement to the playerbase, something to bring them back all at one time and bring life back to the Lands Between's ailing multiplayer invasions and co-operative boss battling.
I still remember how magical the first days of Elden Ring and Shadow of the Erdtree were, the density of asynchronous messages and ease of matchmaking. The Tarnished Edition won't be able to match either of those highs, but its launch may represent the biggest spike in player activity we could ever expect to see in Elden Ring again.
If you've somehow missed the boat on this one since 2022, I envy the first experience you're about to have. Elden Ring's fantasy is somehow both mythic and anthropological, zoomed out, and deeply personal.
(Image credit: FromSoftware) You're an anonymous warrior on a quest to become God's Husband (gender-agnostic). The God in question is a man and woman, separate but the same, consubstantial with, and plotting against themselves. Her pope is a giant turtle , and she is perpetuating a millennia-old conflict involving both racial animus and metaphysics. You can make her goth half- (single? step?) daughter God instead if you so choose.
It's all set in a world of literally impossible beauty, one of the best fantasy settings ever rendered in a videogame. It's dominated by the alien, iconic view of the Erdtree, an ethereal, skyscraper-sized growth that's visible from every part of the Lands Between. Elden Ring is, perhaps, one of FromSoftware's most bright and cheerful creations to date, but it's also one of the weirdest. In four years, it's lodged itself into my psyche like almost no game world I've ever seen.
But enough about all that nerd stuff: FromSoft had already ruined all other 3D action games for me by the time Elden Ring came out, and while it lacks the pure focus of Sekiro's perfect block symphony , I think it matches that more straightforward action game as a fantasy combat experience. Elden Ring is one of the broadest, deepest, and most exquisitely designed action-RPGs that's ever been made.
It even contains Sekiro in a limited sense: One of the character build options added in the Shadow of the Erdtree expansion is a perfect block mechanic lifted straight out of the ninja sim. Like no other game I've played, Elden Ring balances mechanically pure "it's your fault if you die" combat with a myriad of class fantasies and character build options. Knights, barbarians, spellcasters, rogues, priests, samurai, nude men with earthenware hats, you can inhabit any of these roles while engaging in some of the tightest, richest, and most challenging action combat put to silicon.
Which, funnily enough, feeds back into the relatively small additions of the Tarnished Edition DLC: When the mechanics in play are this good, with so much already up in the air, even a minute adjustment feels momentous. FromSoft has not released a full-fledged, solo/async experience like Elden Ring, since Elden Ring, and until it shows off what it's working on next, the Tarnished Edition release will be the closest thing we have to playing a new FromSoft joint at launch.
I have a love/hate/hate relationship with Elden Ring Nightreign , which also no longer seems to be getting updates. In addition to being a Switch 2 exclusive, FromSoft's upcoming Duskbloods looks to have more in common with Nightreign than Bloodborne, firmly in the realm of " a multiplayer thing ." PCG contributor Tyler Colp's sense of FOMO withered on actually playing the game, and mine is rapidly following suit. With no FromSoft fix on the horizon to truly tickle my fancy, I can only turn, once again, to the Lands Between.

title: Thanks to a dedicated team 'art-directing' every single NPC, GTA 6 has over 10 times as many unique animations as GTA 5
text:
There are big-budget blockbusters, and then there's GTA 6. If you want any sense of just how big this thing is, look no further than a recent interview Rockstar North co-head Aaron Garbut gave The New York Times (via Techradar ). In it, he said the studio dedicated an entire new team solely to making NPCs.
"We art-directed each individual one of them," Garbut said in the interview. "Every room in the game, somebody thought about this … Who's sitting where, what they're drinking, the marks that are left on the table. The pictures on the wall will have the people that are in that room, with their tattoos on their arms and their family behind them.
"That whole thing has been made, and built, and photographed, and placed in this random room in a random building in a huge city, in a world." He revealed that GTA 6 has over 600,000 animations—double the amount Red Dead Redemption 2 had, both of which dwarf GTA 5's 55,000. Considering the game's map is also three times as big as Red Dead 2's, it seems like the game operates on an unprecedented level of scale and fidelity.
This all lines up with what PC Gamer's US editor-in-chief Tyler Wilde said of the game in the wake of recent leaks earlier this month : even if GTA 6 doesn't reinvent the open world crime-'em-up, it "will be impressive for the same reason Rockstar games typically are: The absurd amount of effort and money the studio puts into making them as big and detailed as the mainstream hardware of the day can manage."

title: Total War: Warhammer 40,000 wins best PC game at Gamescom
text:
When Total War: Warhammer first debuted, I was much more into the wargame setting's sci-fi counterpart. This would be cool if Space Marines were in it , I remember thinking, somehow unaware that Total War: Warhammer would end up being one of the best strategy games on PC . Not that my theory was wrong: Space Marines are finally in Total War, and it is, in fact, cool. Just ask the folks who picked this year's Gamescom award winners: it won best PC game .
It's the third award Sega took home this year, along with best audio for Alien: Isolation 2 and best lineup for its whole gaggle of games. It's easy to see why, particularly in the case of Total War 40K—PC Gamer's Fraser Brown said it took a mere hour of playtime to cement the game as the highlight of his year . "It's immediately obvious how special Total War 40k is—I don't think a tutorial has ever made me giddy before," he wrote.
According to Gamescom's website, the winners are chosen "by both an expert jury of gaming professionals and the community." In other words, it was a favorite among both professional nerds and the pro bono sort.
If it wasn’t clear before why people have been so vocally insistent that this game should happen ever since Total War first embraced fantasy, it should be now: there are many ways to adapt Warhammer 40,000's galaxy-spanning eternal war in videogame form, but Total War's combination of scale and gruesome, exacting detail seems a particularly good fit.
Warhammer thrives on extremes, and a game where I can watch a single ultramarine hack an ork to bits up close then immediately zoom out to see an enormous whirlwind of violence in wide shot is an exciting prospect indeed. As for whether that'll pan out into a good game once it finally releases, we'll have to wait and see.

title: Star Wars Zero Company's permadeath makes it a better RPG than most RPGs, even though it's not really an RPG
text:
Dungeon Master
(Image credit: Future) Welcome to Dungeon Master , PC Gamer's regular RPG column, where Online Editor Fraser Brown delves into PC gaming's most beloved and enduring genre. This week, Associate Editor Ted Litchfield has subbed in to trade iron short swords and goblins for blaster rifles and clone troopers
When I first tried Star Wars Zero Company for preview, its rhythm reminded me quite a bit of Mass Effect 2: Walk around your home base, upgrade stuff, talk to people, select non-combat activities and missions from a galaxy map, and enter levels that feel "strictly business." Heavy on the combat, with minimal nonviolent gameplay.
It really struck me that Zero Company evolved into this form that has a lot of appeal for the story-heavy RPG fan like myself, but emerged out of a very different, tactics game lineage. That process of reverse-engineering something very RPG-like from a separate but related genre has resulted in a game that I'm not sure the likes of Owlcat, Obsidian, or Larian ever would have made.
Zero Company lacks the branching dialogue trees and minute reactivity of many RPGs, but taking on the apparently herculean task of making even story-centric characters permanently killable has resulted in a game that feels more profoundly reactive and personal than most RPGs I've ever played.
Consequential
One of the coolest things about Zero Company is its simultaneous embrace of permanently missable/killable/losable main characters and triple-A production values, something I think I've only otherwise seen in Baldur's Gate 3, and there only through specific beats of the main story.
In Zero Company, if an operator gets knocked down three times without a stay at the medbay in-between, they're gone for good, no ifs, ands, or buts. Unless you tweak the setting in the game's difficulty—but come on, don't do that. Save scum like a true PC gamer.
(Image credit: Bit Reactor) Zero Company's focus on tactical combat as its north star means you don't see other forms of RPG choice and consequence, like alienating people out of your party in BG3 or Rogue Trader, but being able to permanently miss out on a companion's presence and subplot due to a careless mistake in combat feels more meaningful and personal than many of the authored choices in games I love.
There are very few RPGs that have managed to truly paralyze me with their binary moral choices⁠— Dread Delusion and Cyberpunk 2077: Phantom Liberty spring to mind⁠—but more often, I feel fairly secure in the choices I make in such games, and even stick with them in subsequent playthroughs.
But a true sense of consequence can make things pop even if I know what I want to stick with. Being a commie in Disco Elysium is made richer by the very existence of its fascist playthrough, knowing how dark and depressing the story can get. Kim Kitsuragi's trust and friendship means so much more when you understand it's possible to lose it. Baldur's Gate 3's happiest endings feel almost saccharine to me, but I don't mind, because the bad guy endings are so grim. You have to really work to keep everybody alive by the final party.
Zero Company's companion questlines are excellent, and clone trooper Trick's in particular blew me away. The fact that I have to work to keep Trick alive and see that story makes it feel more my own, even if someone else sees the exact same thing. Bit Reactor has made systemic and authored storytelling compliment each other in a truly novel, rare way. The Fire Emblem series has managed something similar, but not at this level of production values (full voice acting!) or with a cast so closely intertwined with the main plot.
Loss leader
(Image credit: Bit Reactor) If there's anything I want Bit Reactor to do next, it's to even more tightly wind the threat of permanent loss into the plot. It's not possible to piss off squadmates enough that they leave your crew through the Bond (approval) system in Zero Company. I would love to see that wrench thrown into things in Bit Reactor's next project.
There are story moments in Zero Company that genuinely imperil or drive away your companions: I want to see even more of that. Zero Company's permadeath is a unique melding of story and gameplay in the current field, but otherwise, the game's story and gameplay are fairly siloed from each other. The non-combat operations and exploration gameplay have fairly limited effects on the story and tactical side of things: You take on a mission, or you don't. You have access to new resources, or you lack them.
With more time, resources, and experience making this sort of game, I would love for Bit Reactor's next project to be even more of an RPG, to embrace consequence and reactivity even more deeply. It's already a phenomenal first outing , and I can't wait to see what's next.

title: A Star Wars Galaxies community server was allegedly hacked with AI assistance by a Reddit moderator harboring a primeval grudge
text:
Star Wars Galaxies Legends, one of many community servers offering a version of the defunct MMO with custom additions, reportedly had its assets decrypted by a hacker with the username levarrishawk (via Massively OP ). In a post on the Star Wars Galaxies subreddit, Levarris confirmed the details of a Discord post shared by the server's development team.
"[W]e’ve confirmed that Levarris, aka levarrishawk from r/swg, used AI tools to decrypt our client side game asset files," the Discord post reads. "This gave him access to assets from all of our custom content: items, questlines … We do know that he’s actively offered these files to other servers, and while we can’t confirm that he’s had any takers yet, if you start seeing Legends‑exclusive content out in other worlds it was likely taken from us.
"We’re obviously bothered by this, but there isn’t much we can do outside of being upfront with all of you and staying focused on what makes Legends great."
Notably, no player data or personal info was accessed. The response from Levarris, who is a moderator for the Star Wars Galaxies subreddit, reveals the motivation behind this hack: some drama that goes back "roughly fourteen years ago."
Levarris claims that some folks who'd eventually work on Legends used a "honeypot" scheme to acquire dev tools that Sony Online Entertainment used when working on the live game, and then didn't share those tools with other community devs trying to revive it. "You don't get to protect and hoard from the greater community things built on stolen goods," Levarris wrote.
The subreddit didn't seem impressed with the stunt nor the rationale behind it. "I’m just trying to play around with a lightsaber after working 60 hours in a week," commented iceman2kx. "A moderator of the Star Wars Galaxies subreddit has decided to actively harm the Star Wars Galaxies community at large. Cool. Cool and good," BroReesta wrote on the same thread.

title: 'Sidequests are almost my reason for doing videogames in the first place:' The dev behind one of the coolest upcoming RPGs says its word count is ballooning because they just love side stories so much
text:
The early access RPG Entropy would be cool enough in a vacuum: Experimental, JRPG-style combat in a bizarre, fallen world. But it's also a second outing from the devs of one of my favorite RPGs in recent memory, Dread Delusion.
Dread Delusion was a first-person homage to the Elder Scrolls that, true to its inspirations, had some absolutely killer sidequests, like an ethical dilemma surrounding vegetarian zombies or a seemingly Blade Runner 2049-inspired investigation into a person erased from history (and their loved ones' memories). With Entropy's subgenre shift, I wondered if developer Lovely Hellplace would keep up this side stuff streak.
I needn't have worried: Speaking recently with lead developer James Wragg, he told me in no uncertain terms that he and the team can't help themselves. They love sidequests too much to not make them.
"Side quests are almost my reason for doing videogames in the first place," Wragg told me. "A big inspiration for Dread Delusion was playing Elder Scrolls games almost willfully ignoring the main quest, and getting lost in all the side content."
Wragg finds that RPGs really come alive in their side stories, partially because they're allowed to be strange, and to provide a contrast with the main plot. Wragg estimated that he wrote "about a third" of what's gone into Entropy, and that he likes to create outlines or broad strokes directions for areas and plotlines that other writers then fill in.
He praised Dread Delusion writer Harry Tuffs for bringing the zombified Kingdom of the Endless to life in exactly this way: "I knew the Endless were going to be like, vegetarian vampires," said Wragg, "and I gave this to Harry, and he made it way better than my original dumb ideas."
Wragg also shouted out returning writer Io Brindle, who spearheaded that investigative quest I loved so much in Dread Delusion, Missing Persons. Even still, before starting Entropy, Wragg had a notion that it would be less verbose than Dread Delusion⁠.
"I started off Entropy with the idea that we were going to write way fewer words," Wragg said. "I was like, 'Dread Delusion is like the length of a novel. This is crazy. This took so much work.' So for Entropy, I really wanted to cut the word count down loads. We were going to trim the fat and make it more succinct.
"As we've been writing it, we've found that we just like really getting into characters, and we just like fleshing stuff out with interesting themes, and that does actually take a fair amount of words."
Even though it will take a significant lift from Entropy's writing team, Wragg sounded more excited than anything else, and believes that Entropy's side content will hit the same high marks with players as Dread Delusion's.
Lovely Hellplace, DreadXP Lovely Hellplace, DreadXP Lovely Hellplace, DreadXP Lovely Hellplace, DreadXP Lovely Hellplace, DreadXP Some of this writing work is also being put toward companions: Entropy has a large party size and allows for hiring more anonymous mercenary characters, but there are also story-centric party members with their own plotlines. All of them, mercenary or story-based, will be subject to permadeath, something I loved in the recently-released Star Wars Zero Company .
"We love making weird and wonderful stories, and we love deep characters who we can get into chats with and find out all their beliefs and backstories and stuff," said Wragg. "I think that one of the most interesting things about videogames is just how you can actually talk to the characters in a way that maybe you can't in a novel or a film. Just being able to meet a strange character and ask them some stupid questions is incredibly rewarding as a player."
Entropy is out now on Steam in early access for the very reasonable price of $12/£8.99, and it also has a quite generous demo that won me over to the game months ago . If Dread Delusion is anything to go by, the final game will see a significant expansion over this initial release, but I found Dread Delusion's initial early access launch to be a great introduction to the project.

title: Steam Week in Review: Here are the top 10 most popular genres on Steam
text:
A ridiculous amount of games release on Steam every week and basically none of them make any money. It only takes a cursory browse of Steam's unfiltered new release list to understand why this is true.
But which genre is most likely to make money or be a hit? Ichiro Lambe, Matt Martindale and Dr. Tim Ermilov have collaborated on a Steam revenue report on weloveit.io and, as the name implies, the purpose of the site is to estimate the earnings of all Steam games, or at least, those with a price tag and at least one review.
The trio doesn't have access to Valve's internal sales data, so they rely on the Boxleiter method to estimate that data, which assumes that a games' review count is "roughly proportional of its sales, so multiplying reviews by a constant gives an estimated unit count." For a standard estimate (rather than a conservative or generous one) the multiplier is 35 times the amount of user reviews.
This may not provide exact figures, but as the site notes, it's a technique used by analysts and publishers and there aren't very many better ways to arrive at a sales estimate. And so, in the style of all great data enthusiasts, they've used the technique to map the success (or lack thereof) of over 100,000 Steam games in handy graph form.
Baldur's Gate 3 is estimated to have made $1,795,480,003 since its early access launch in late 2020. On the other hand Free Solo, a physics climbing game released in March, has made an estimated $34.
In the graph below every dot is an individual game (for a much better view of this graph you'll need to visit weloveit.io ).
(Image credit: weloveit.io) I was fascinated by the "genre economics" section, which uses user tags to get a sense of how genres rank on Steam. "A game counts towards a genre only when the tag is one of its six most popular tags," according to the study, so there needs to be pretty unanimous agreement among Steam users that the tag is accurate.
According to the data, sandbox games have the highest "hit rate" on Steam. Hit rate measures the amount of games with the tag that have made more than $100k. The sandbox tag has a 27.3% hit rate.
Of course,"sandbox" is unwieldy and impractical as a genre designation: the most popular games with the tag are unhelpfully different: Terraria, Red Dead Redemption 2 and Project Zomboid. But it does at least demonstrate that games promising some amount of freedom are preferred by Steam users, whether they be sloppy retail sims or $400 million cowboy adventures.
The next tag, FPS, is probably the "real" genre winner. It has a 21.6% hit rate, though keep in mind a lot of games that aren't strictly focused on shooting, like Schedule I or Portal 2, are tagged with FPS.

There aren't a huge amount of surprises in that list. I guess I'm surprised to see visual novels rank so highly, though they are ubiquitous on Steam. Sports probably ranks highly because there are fewer games to which it applies compared to, say, "puzzle", a tag with a 9.5% hit rate.
The lowest ranking tags (according to report's list, at least) are probably more telling. Hidden Object games have a 5.4% hit rate, while 2D platformers have a 5.5% hit rate. Developing a game in either of those genres is thus, according to the study, risky business. Though they may also be cheaper to develop, and thus more common, and thus less likely to be discovered.
The full study is well worth browsing because it's full of great insights. For example: 2D platformers have severely dropped off in popularity since their heyday of 2016, but visual novels have remained almost consistently popular since 2014.

First of all, its worth noting that Star Wars Zero Company released on the 28th, and its review embargo lifted on the 26th, so next week's chart will better reflect its launch performance. It still came in at number 12, rising 12 positions for what must have been an eleventh hour rush on pre-orders (there were cosmetic pre-order incentives).
Based on the chart—which is, as always, a reflection of best performers by revenue and not necessarily by units sold—Mortal Shell 2 had a successful launch, but probably no where near as successful as How to Fish. The latter is a 1-4 player "physics-based fishing simulator, and while it looks like quintessential friendslop on the surface, it's a whole lot more violent than normal. It looks very fun .
The Wardogs beta obviously paid off as a taster for the full game, which releases next month. As for Stalker 2, it got a massive 2.0 update last week and a steep discount, hence its reappearance on the list.

This ticks a lot of boxes. A grimy cement-filled eastern European setting? Check. Scrappy first-person combat with a focus on managing scarcity? Yep. Terrifying things to shoot at? Of course. People in the Steam comments are comparing it to No More Room in Hell and ZombiU (remember that?).
Aggelos 2 | August 28
A surprise sequel to the cheerful 2018 Wonder Boy clone, Aggelos 2 seems to double down on the metroidvania elements: there are "two massive, overlapping maps" here spread across two parallel realms. Like its predecessor, this 16-bit styled platformer isn't very original, but if you love the art style like I do, that'll be beside the point.
Can I Come In? | August 28
This is a short and sweet first-person horror set in a neighbourhood of Soviet era tower blocks. You're a teenager left alone for the evening, and as you can imagine, it's not destined to be a peaceful night. This one's less than a fiver and runs to around an hour.
Divinum | August 29
Yet another metroidvania. Divinum, like Aggelos 2 above, isn't the most original offering but the presentation is evocative, and the hack 'n' slash inspired combat looks finely honed. Protagonist Fjør is on a mission to save her northern homeland from some unspecified evil, which means lots of running, jumping, and cartoon violence.

title: 1666: Amsterdam's developer says it 'won't be using any AI anymore', and the tech was only used 'in conception and pre-production'—arguably the most creative phase of the entire process
text:
There was surprise and delight when Summer Game Fest brought the reveal of 1666: Amsterdam , the long awaited dream project from Assassin's Creed co-creator Patrice Désilets. But the mood quickly changed when eager players began exploring a playable prologue for the witchy action-adventure that was released alongside the announcement and began spotting in-game assets that had the distinct whiff of generative AI.
Désilets' studio Panache Digital Games copped to using AI in the production of certain assets, then apologised and promised to remove those elements in time for the early access launch. With that launch happening last week, Désilets now says that Panache has decoupled AI from its pipeline entirely and it won't be using AI in future.
Speaking to GamesRadar+ , Désilets stressed that Panache was done with generative AI, and claimed that most of the AI used occurred in the early stages of the project. "Yes, we use some AI in the process, mostly at the beginning," Désilets explained. "In conception and pre-production. It's been totally removed and we won't be using any AI anymore."
As someone who likes their art made by, y'know, artists, I'm glad that Panache has done what it can to scrape generative AI out of 1666: Amsterdam. That said, it irks me when developers say they only used AI at the concepting stage of development, because that's the most fun and rewarding part of any creative project.
That's the part where most of the imaginative work happens, where you're most creatively free and unshackled from the discipline and hard choices required to actually finish the darn thing. Handing that phase over to the mediocrity machine seems like such a betrayal of the creative process to me. It also raises an interesting philosophical point: can you reasonably say a game has no generative AI in it if you used the technology to help imagine the thing in the first place?
Either way, 1666: Amsterdam is now out in early access, and the Steam page does not have an AI disclosure on it. With or without AI, players currently seem divided over Amsterdam as an experience. The game currently sits at a 'Mixed' rating with 66% positive reviews, with users praising the setting and exploration elements, while cruising clunky combat and a general lack of polish.

title: The Steam 'teraleak' extends far beyond Valve games, including prototypes of third-party titles like Mafia 2 and Grand Theft Auto 3: 'This may be one of if not the biggest leaks to occur'
text:
On Saturday, information began circulating online about a massive, 12-terabyte leak of Valve data that included prototypes of numerous classic Valve games. But it seems what is now being dubbed the "teraleak" contained far more than just old builds of Portal 2 and possible weapons from Half-Life 2: Episode 3, and may include prototypes of countless third-party games released on Steam over a ten-year period.
Specifically, the leak consists of Steam file groups known as 'depots' which were stored on Steam's servers between 2003 and 2013. A full list of these depots was shared on Reddit by user RefreshingCapybara, which includes depot names for hundreds of games as well as trailers, teasers, soundtracks, demos, game trials, and more. "Not to be hyperbolic, but this may be one of if not the biggest leaks to occur," RefreshingCapybara commented in sharing the list.
To be clear, the list doesn't show us what—if anything—is contained within those file groups. But as reported by Ars Technica , game preservation website Hidden Palace has identified numerous depots with obtainable builds in them. These include various prototypes of Spec Ops: The Line , Sid Meier's Civilization V , Mafia 2 , and Grand Theft Auto 3 .
According to Ars, it's also likely that the builds included in the leak are from a collection that has been amassed from various sources over time. Many game builds from before 2013—which is when Valve switched its content distribution pipeline from Steam2 to SteamPipe—were considered lost media up to now. Clearly, though, they were more accessible than Valve or anyone else realised.
As such, it's possible the leak is the product of multiple people pulling together builds from various sources (like old PCs) into one enormous archive. The most interesting clue to the leak's origins is a readme file contained within the leak, which includes the line "warm n good wishes to all hoarders who had stuff from this collection".
The fact that the build includes so many third-party prototypes may also make it legally perilous. "That archive contains a significant amount of third-party content, meaning we are dealing with a dramatically more dangerous situation than if it were just some Valve builds," wrote YouTuber and Valve specialist Tyler McVicker on social media.
Given the sheer amount of data that has been leaked, it will likely be some time before we know the true extent of what it contains. On the Valve side, dataminers have already unearthed a complete version of Portal 2's 2009 "beta", as well as prototypes for Left 4 Dead , Counter-Strike: Global Offensive , and even some files from Valve's cancelled puzzler F-STOP.

title: A 38-year-old NES platformer is getting a Steam remake by its original husband-and-wife team, as the pair's 'final major game product'
text:
Games get remade for all sorts of reasons, but I think you'd struggle to find one with as heartwarming a basis as this. The Battle of Olympus —a side-scrolling platformer originally released on the NES in 1988, is getting a remake early next year created by its original husband-and-wife team.
Admittedly, that statement is slightly misleading. Per Time Extension , programmer Yukio Horimoto and artist Reiko Oshida (now also Horimoto) were not actually married when they made The Battle of Olympus—though they were in a romantic relationship at the time of the game's development.
"We fell in love and wanted to make our game together, so we talked about the game concept for a long time," Horimoto explained to VG247 in an interview from several years back. "I like Greek myths and legends, so we decided to base our game on those legends. Given those circumstances, we talked about the game and our mood influenced it."
Alongside Greek myth, The Battle of Olympus is heavily inspired by The Legend of Zelda 2, with Horimoto stating that he directly imitated many of that game's actions. " I wanted to make the same kind of game, and so many parts of the game, like the player's attacking motion, ducking motion, and jumping motion: They were all influenced by The Legend of Zelda."
As for the remake, the Steam page describes it as a "handcrafted Steam remake", with Yukio and Reiko Horimoto's reformed Infinity Co "personally recreated in the code, redrawing the pixel art, and refining the game for modern PC players while preserving the spirit, atmosphere and challenge of the original."
Interestingly, this isn't the first time a veteran game developer couple has remade a gaming classic. A few years back, Sierra founders Ken and Roberta Williams returned to game development for a shiny redux of Colossal Cave Adventure (with the abridged name Colossal Cave ). Unlike The Battle of Olympus, Colossal Cave wasn't the Williams' original design. The OG text adventure was made in the mid '70s by Will Crowther and Don Woods.
Like the Williams', Yukio and Reiko Horimoto have been fairly active in game development in recent years, having directed the fashion model sims Model Debut #nicola and its sequel in 2019 and 2021. It seems the pair plan to retire from game development for good after the The Battle of Olympus, however, as the Steam page says the remake will be the duo's "final major game product".
The Battle of Olympus will release into Steam early access in January 2027.

title: Fable's story will be '15-20 hours' long, according to its game director, although the game's life systems are 'limitless'
text:
Throughout all of Fable 's showcases and demonstrations this year, one aspect of it has proved difficult to figure out—how big it's going to be. The original Fable games were decently-sized, but not massive, and monster roleplaying games like Elden Ring and Baldur's Gate 3 have dramatically shifted expectations on what an RPG's scope should be.
But it turns out that Fable will stick closely to tradition when it comes to its size, with the caveat that players could potentially hang around in Playground's RPG forever depending on how invested they become in the world they help to forge.
Speaking to Polygon in a Q&A session, associate game director Will Kennedy explained that Fable will have a total of around 40 hours of things to do in the world. "We have around 15-20 hours of mainline quest gameplay, we have around 15-20 of side and open-world exploration content gameplay," Kennedy said.
That's the traditional baseline for an RPG. But Kennedy also pointed out that Fable's life-systems, which allow players to interact with NPCs, commit crimes, buy property and so forth may significantly expand the runtime. "And then, of course, the life systems are limitless, so you can play them for as long as you want." To this, fellow associate game director Craig Litter added that "You can literally play it forever if that's what you want to do."
It's worth stating at this point that you can play any game forever if you really want to do that. I could probably play Doom forever even though the base game is not all that long. Nonetheless, if Fable's life simulation elements put it within touching distance of, say, The Sims, then maybe the 'play it forever' claim isn't so far-fetched.
We were expecting to find out how Fable shapes up relatively soon. But Playground's long-awaited RPG has been pushed to 2027 in order to avoid the looming behemoth that is Grand Theft Auto 6 . Alongside its life simulation, the reboot is swapping out the series' old morality system for a more nuanced, character-specific reputation system, although you'll apparently be able to bypass it if you're rich enough —just like in real life!

title: The Blood of Dawnwalker review
text:
Need to know
What is it? A Witchery vampire RPG with a dark heart
Release date September 3, 2026
Expect to pay $70 / £60
Developer Rebel Wolves
Publisher Bandai Namco
Reviewed on RTX 3060 (laptop), Ryzen 5 5600H, 16GB RAM
Steam Deck TBC, but unlikely to be a good experience
Link Steam
35 hours into The Blood of Dawnwalker I'd already witnessed the aftermath of many barbaric slayings and village razings. I'd cleared out a site of industrial-scale slaughter, and partaken in an obscene medieval take on The Running Man. I'd sucked countless kiloliters of blood from humans, rats and monsters alike. But somehow, this exceptionally morbid horror RPG still had another novel way to make me wince.
I was exploring the depths of a troll-infected cave deep in the Carpathians. Coen of Laslea—me, the player-character—and his sketchy companion were looking for someone important. I hardly expected them to be living well, but the way I found them, pinned to a wall and half-consumed, exceeded my expectations for mainstream videogame cruelty.
For two years this human-shaped creature had been constantly eaten alive by grotesque kobalds. By dint of being a vampire, their flesh always grew back. They were a wall-mounted, self-replenishing feast of human meat, lost in a network of caves where they were unlikely to ever be found.
The Blood of Dawnwalker is one of the best blockbuster action RPGs I've played for years, probably since Elden Ring, but it's unrelentingly violent and bleak to the point of sometimes being unintentionally funny. There is no hope in Rebel Wolves' blood-slurried take on 1300s Romania, where brutal feudalism has been supplanted by populist vampirism. The Witcher 3 feels like daytime melodrama by comparison. I respect its severity, but I did yearn for a gutful of the Transylvanian white wine crowding my inventory.
Eerie vrakhiri
When we meet him, Coen is an everyman peasant working the land in Laslea. Years ago, Skender Dragosti, the murderous lord who formerly ruled over Laslea and the greater Vale Sangora region, had been conquered by Brencis, a century-old warfaring vrakhir, or vampire, sick of watching all that blood go to waste.
I can boil the Brencis' blood, temporarily extract their souls, scream at them until they're immobile, or possess them, all the better to turn them to my side.
Brencis is not as outwardly cruel as Skender but his manner of industrially harvesting the blood of Sangora's peasants is frowned upon by some, while for others it's a reasonable price to pay for the execution of their former oppressor. But when the slightest hint of resistance is detected in Laslea, Brencis and his men swoop on the village, raze it, and abduct Coen's family. The Blood of Dawnwalker is about trying to get them back and, to varying degrees depending on your choices and temperament, also taking the fight to the vrakhiri.
Which is easier than it might otherwise be for a peasant, because Coen soon becomes a Dawnwalker: vampire by night and regular human by day. In this way, Rebel Wolves has its cake and eats it too. Coen can fight with swords at all times, but witchcraft and vampire powers can only be used by day and night respectively. He doesn't need to cower in the shadows at sundown. He's a very versatile bloodsucker.
It's great fun to slay Brencis' men. Coen's swordplay is similar to Kingdom Come's directional approach: I have to pay attention to how my foe is swinging all the better to block in that direction, and then exploit any weakness this opens up. This can be gruelling in the realism-focused Kingdom Come, but it's much more approachable here, thanks to an icon signalling every incoming move that's visible no matter how close or far the enemy is (this can be toggled off at higher difficulties).
Rebel Wolves Rebel Wolves It's also more approachable because I can trigger hectic waves of spectral crows in between strikes, or warp behind my enemies to suck their blood and replenish my health. I can boil the Brencis' blood, temporarily extract their souls, scream at them until they're immobile, or possess them, all the better to turn them to my side.
Like The Witcher 3 before it, The Blood of Dawnwalker borrows a lot from the quietly radical combat approach taken by Rocksteady's Batman games. Like Geralt of Rivia, Coen "sticks" to and circle-strafes his primary target, but unlike Geralt of Rivia, Coen's swordplay is precision-oriented and gratifying, albeit maybe a little too easy for hardened players. The lock on system can be imprecise—it's always a pain on rare occasions when I want to choose an enemy rather than let the targeting choose for me—but I actually went out of my way to fight people and monsters, rather than avoid conflict like I thought I would (and which I mostly can't, anyway). It helps that Coen's skill trees are riddled with some truly overpowered delights.
(Image credit: Rebel Wolves) Days gone
But it takes time to hone these skills, not to mention all the other minor and major perks and buffs in each of Dawnwalker's three skill trees. And time is framed as a crucial currency in The Blood of Dawnwalker. Coen's days are separated into 16 units of time, and nearly everything I do—from completing major quests through to levelling up my bloodsucking prowess—spends one or more units.
And my quest is urgent: Brencis' coronation occurs in 30 days, and that's my deadline for saving my family. After that they're done for. Little wonder I don't want to fetch slivovitz for one of my dad's old war mates.
(Image credit: Rebel Wolves) This pressure feels overwhelming at first. Should I prioritise assassinating Brencis' three vassals, all the better to weaken the regime for a (presumed) final showdown? Is it really a good idea to spend my time doing the bidding of local witch and love interest Anca? As Dawnwalker's early hours wore on, a handful of other urgencies emerged to complicate how Coen should spend his precious time, not least the fact that some tasks can only be completed by day or night.
By day 20 my Coen felt virtually unbeatable, and I had a small handful of promising ways to take the fight to Brencis.
The concept is similar to Persona and Majora's Mask, but the way it's implemented is the glue holding Dawnwalker's jumble of familiar components neatly together. It encourages a more tactical approach to questing than I'm used to in action RPGs: I often found myself browsing my journal and plotting out how I'd make the next couple of days matter. This didn't always involve heroics. For example, by day I'd buy up manuals from nine-to-five vendors, all the better to learn new skills, because spending skill points passes time. By night, with my vampiric shadowstep ability, I could access rooftops or cliff shelves inaccessible to mortals. Sometimes my plans would be waylaid by the sudden emergence of a time sensitive problem.
The calendar system sure does apply urgency to Coen's task, at least at first. Urgency is almost always baked into the narrative of blockbuster RPGs, but it's problematic to reflect that urgency in actual gameplay systems. Sure I want to save the world, and sure I want for my actions to matter. But I'd also like to pick some nirnroot and play some Gwent, thank you very much. There’s a reason the Pathologic games remain a niche concern.
(Image credit: Rebel Wolves) Rebel Wolves tries to sidestep this problem in a couple of ways. First, the player is always amply warned before embarking on a time-spending activity: I can waste as many IRL hours as I like harvesting St John's-wort and the position of the sun or moon won't change. It takes me knowingly triggering the passage of time for my precious hours to be spent.
Second, the pressure is largely illusory. By day 20 my Coen felt virtually unbeatable, and I had a small handful of promising ways to take the fight to Brencis. Maybe I could have fetched that old bastard his slivovitz after all.
But illusory or not—and it'll likely depend on how much you drag your feet—the calendar system does give Dawnwalker a greater sense of choice and consequence than most of its big budget action contemporaries. It's largely up to me how I'm going to save my family, when I'll do it, in which order I'll take measures to make it easier, or if I'll bother at all. But I can't deny it was deflating to discover that all my careful clock strategising was ultimately for nothing: pretty much everything of any importance can be tied up well before the 30 day deadline, with lots of frivolous traipsing around to boot.
(Image credit: Rebel Wolves) Despite this, it feels like Rebel Wolves learned the right lessons from Breath of the Wild or, before it, Gothic: Dawnwalker provides an explicit goal and then gestures vaguely at its world. Completing quests can either teach or strengthen Coen, but he has to find them first, and this is where players' experiences may vary. I was on day 21, and pretty much ready to stick it to Brencis, when a colleague let slip that there was a major companion whose presence and attendant quest had eluded me for 30 hours.
Quests vary in size and interest. Some are long and winding; others amount to "kill these guys" or "follow these glowing yellow hints to an encounter". I definitely got sick of searching for yellow hints, just as I did rotating an object for points of revelatory interest. But I never got sick of fighting, nor did I ever lose interest in the Vale of Sangora itself.
All in vein
Maybe I'm just a sucker for European miserablism, but The Blood of Dawnwalker's valley of bloodletting is one of my favourite open worlds since The Witcher 3. Its take on 1300s Romania is subtly daubed with fantasy, but like CD Projekt, Rebel Wolves has a knack for gorgeously downcast panoramas. Though Coen can move at lightning speed by dint of his vampire powers (by night he can even transform into a galloping wolf), I often found myself slow-walking the fir forest backroads and alpine highlands of Sangora, taking in sights reminiscent of Caspar David Friedrich's landscape paintings or the covers of Tolkien-themed black metal albums. Though it’s not immune to open world busywork, Dawnwalker at least knows its open world needs to feel like a world and not a sandbox of mini-games. It’s a place I inhabited, rather than a map I traversed towards quests and rewards.
Rebel Wolves Rebel Wolves Rebel Wolves Rebel Wolves Rebel Wolves Rebel Wolves And like The Witcher 3, Rebel Wolves keeps a tighter leash on its fantastical leanings than most fantasy studios. Supernatural themes regularly puncture the bleak and rugged realism—this is, of course, a vampire game—but the fantasy elements only serve to emphasise the humdrum nastiness of the Sangora peasants' lot: this is a world of hand-to-mouth poverty, tyrannous cruelty and materialised superstition. The latter almost feels like a delirious symptom of the former. I highly doubt Dawnwalker is an authentic rendering of 1300s peasant life in Romania or elsewhere, but it is determined to capture the phantasmagoric mystery of pre-enlightenment, and the horror and indignity of an oppressed people, without resorting to folksiness or misplaced nostalgia.
My allegiances—or rather, my notion of who was the worst of various competing evils—were in constant flux.
Boy, is this an unremittingly pessimistic experience. Choices are almost invariably between two evils. Quests move inexorably towards bad or worse endings. Rarely did I ever select a dialogue option with complete confidence that it was the right or magnanimous thing to say. In fact, by the end, I had my Coen acting very much at odds with how I envisioned him in the early hours. My allegiances—or rather, my notion of who was the worst of various competing evils—were in constant flux. I experienced three endings (there are more) and not one of them offered any hope.
And this is what I admire most about The Blood of Dawnwalker. In the opening hours it clocks as an almost on-the-nose allegory for 20th century European history—Brencis equals incoming communism, Skender equals outgoing monarchy—but by the end it registers as a more universally human story about the vile extremes of power, the powerlessness of its subjects, and the latter's susceptibility to persuasion when nothing feels real except tragedy and toil. It's also—and I find myself sometimes forgetting this aspect entirely—a vampire story. None of its narrative components are especially original, but they cohere into something viscerally affecting. There is no morally righteous way to solve the problems of this world.
(Image credit: Rebel Wolves) It's a very well optimised game too. On my unimpressive system I was generally able to stick to 60 fps on low at 1080p, and even at these settings I found Dawnwalker gorgeous.
Life drain
It's understandable to feel exhausted after playing Dawnwalker, despite its relatively modest 40 hour runtime. It can be so doggedly miserable that you just have to laugh at it, and I did laugh occasionally, but not for the rare and minor sparks of light. When these occur, it feels like being shaken from a disturbing dream. I mostly laughed for shock at its audacity. There are no heroes here. Everything, always, sucks . I learned nothing, but I felt a lot.
(Image credit: Rebel Wolves) Blood of Dawnwalker is an effective piece of worldbuilding and storytelling then, but it doesn't make good on its promise as an innovative piece of RPG design. Maybe Rebel Wolves worried that too many players would fall afoul of the passage of time and thus loosened its severity. Certainly, the prologue implies a greater role for this system than what eventuates. In the end, Dawnwalker doesn't have the courage to allow this system to show its fangs. I feel like if it did, we’d have a modern classic on our hands.
It also suffers some commonplace open world trappings. There are lots of icons denoting almost identical tasks. There are Ubisoft-style towers to scale. The freedom of fast travel tends to diminish the scale of the world with time (why doesn't fast travel incur a time cost?).
But I mention these shortcomings out of a sense of almost begrudging responsibility: despite its obvious indebtedness to The Witcher, The Blood of Dawnwalker is a distinctly dismal horror RPG whose unyielding darkness and sense of benighted adventure will leave more of an impression than any of its flaws. I hope this series gets the chance to return with a fiercer appetite for my blood.

title: Onimusha: Way of the Sword review
text:
Miyamoto Musashi, the legend goes, defeated his rival Sasaki Ganryu with a single blow to the head using nothing but a crude wooden sword carved from an oar.
Need to Know
What is it? The art of swordplay, revolutionized after the discovery of physics
Release date September 3, 2026
Expect to pay $70/£60
Developer Capcom
Publisher Capcom
Reviewed on Radeon RX 9070 XT, Intel i5-13600K, 64GB DDR5
Steam Deck Playable
Link Official site
This is, of course, ridiculous: In truth Musashi first parried dozens of Ganryu's strikes, softened him up with a flourish of reflex combos, and then ran him through with the Flashing Void, a spear harnessed from the power of lightning in an ancient demonic hellforge. He was perhaps a bit too modest to recount the more baroque details of the battle in his memoirs, but blessedly Capcom is less bashful.
Onimusha: Way of the Sword whips ass.
I've been told that two words don't qualify as a review, though, so let's talk caveats. I'd put the action in this long, long-awaited reboot up against the best Capcom's ever made, though it's spread out across a 10K that should be a sprint. It begins with a foundation of weighty swordplay that made me feel the muscle and bone behind each strike, and eventually challenged me to parry increasingly ostentatious bosses with a patience and precision I haven't exercised since Sekiro. The reward each and every time was the exhilaration of locking in and nailing the timing, graduating from a quick game over to a calm, clean execution.
Well, not that calm—other than the adrenaline a few of Onimusha's harder fights left pulsing in my hypothalamus, this game sets itself apart from FromSoftware's taciturn tone with a swagger reminiscent of early 2000s Capcom. One of its great strengths is the use of legendary actor Toshiro Mifune's likeness as Musashi, an act of digital necromancy that could've easily left a rotten stink if it wasn't handled precisely this deftly. But it doesn't just work, it makes the game.
Capcom Capcom Capcom Capcom Capcom Capcom Capcom I loved Onimusha's lavishly animated cutscenes just as much as the combat: Musashi is brash, fiery, and incredibly expressive, tilting his head with a cocky boast, cartoonishly gawping at monsters, contorting his whole face into a snarl when he gets his blood up. A throwaway moment where he scratches the back of his head exactly like the real Mifune does so much to make Way of the Sword feel like an homage to bloody '70s samurai flicks down to its bones.
Onimusha needed to nail that authenticity, because the dozen samurai roles I've seen Mifune in add up to significantly less screen time than the 35-odd hours I spent finishing the story and a healthy chunk of sidequests. Too long? Yep! Unfortunately the Capcom that made Resident Evil 9 and Pragmata lean, briskly paced adventures wasn't talking to the Capcom that thought Onimusha needed a dull hub world, grindy crafting materials and bosses that show up for an encore to an encore to an encore well after I stopped applauding.
Kyoto drift
Capcom Capcom Capcom Capcom There's a distinct whiff of modern videogame bloat to Way of the Sword compared to the tight 3 ½ and 8 ½ hours of the now-vintage Onimusha 1&2. It spends its first third steadily introducing new combat mechanics and devoting quite a bit of time to how a young, not-yet-famous Musashi finds himself wearing a magic gauntlet that absorbs the souls of the demonic Genma trying to move into east Kyoto. The initial pacing means it's slow to really show its teeth, though I found that a nice change from the soulslikes that are now legion.
Onimusha wants you to feel cool from the start: Duels with the basic Genma tend to feel more empowering than challenging, which narratively dovetails nicely with Musashi's gauntlet steroids but means only boss fights really allow the swordplay to shine until the midgame.
(Image credit: Capcom) In between major plot beats that whisk Musashi off to new environments like a bamboo grove and a sunset-drenched mountain fortress, there's busywork to do in feudal Kyoto. And it sure is bogged down by dreary, muddy streets that immediately blur together. There are engaging moments here and there when a trinket on the other side of a wall enticed me to find a ladder that led to a hidden crawlspace to a gate I could unlock from the inside, but these detours never really rose above the bar of not outright boring .
Kyoto mostly exists as a vessel for upgrade materials, scattered in plain sight and squirreled away in corners that are occasionally more fun to track down. These items and the gangs of Genma roving the streets respawn periodically, which ended up reinforcing how insignificant most of my time spent in Kyoto felt. Same with the trifling basic sidequests, delivered by nameless NPCs that give you an icon on the map; there's not even an attempt to offer hints for you to puzzle out a location yourself.
Oni-curious
You can sense the nervousness behind this whole side of the game: that players needed something to keep them playing longer, so how about collecting dozens and dozens of pieces of leather and iron to upgrade the stats on their gear 2% at a time? What about an exciting boss that gets some new moves the second time, and then really drags down the pacing each time you fight it again? Even Capcom seemed to know it didn't nail the balance here, considering how many times the writers have Musashi grumble about having to fight someone he's already whooped.
Strip out 90% of the upgrade economy and corresponding time spent in Kyoto and Onimusha: Way of the Sword would be a much leaner game. And a better one, with just a brisk hour or so of scraps in between showstopper bosses.
(Image credit: Capcom) What saves Kyoto from being a total waste are the Curious Cases, a fancier set of sidequests delivered to Musashi by poet Lady Murasaki, a pioneering 11th century author.
These vignettes are a touch more involved, calling on a recurring cast of Kyoto's citizens to deliver morbidly funny Japanese fables. Each concludes with Murasaki commenting on the story as she writes them into legend. I rarely go digging into a menu to read up on extra lore, but I devoured every bit of it in Onimusha—the care put into the mythology does so much to make this feel like a jidaigeki historical drama as much as an action game. There are only a handful of Curious Cases in the whole game, yet they each left more of an impression on me than any sidequest I encountered in 25 hours with last year's Assassin's Creed Shadows.
Sword is life
Onimusha's crafting-driven bloat would've annoyed me more if every boss that awaited wasn't such a thrill to take down. The heavy clank of steel-on-steel and the way the camera pivots around Musashi as he redirects the enemy's blade in a shower of sparks was still triggering something primal within me 30 hours in. (Should I buy a sword? Surely a katana would fix me.)
The elegance of the combat is that each duel demands the same thing—precisely parrying a few times to build up a "burning" meter for your blade to deal more damage, then using the deflect technique, an extra button press with slightly more generous timing, to sap the enemy's stamina and deliver a critical hit—but executing that plan is never so simple. When I fumbled my parry timing and blocked instead, bosses punished me by smashing my own stamina meter, turning the fight into an oh shit oh hell panic.
(Image credit: Capcom) Take one of the minibosses that Onimusha reheats three too many times: Byakue, a demon carrying a giant axe whose entire body is covered in ofuda talismans. When Byakue broke my guard, its axe split in half to reveal a jagged maw that sucked down souls and sent it into a primal rage. I learned to start watching for new moves in that state: a grab where it used its flowing paper-flesh mane to bludgeon me, and an explosive slam that caused the earth to erupt with poisonous Malice.
Where other action games like Nioh ask you to nail multiple complex button inputs in the heat of the moment to parry, recover stamina, and swap sword stances, Onimusha's happy to keep swordplay simpler mechanically but more cinematically rewarding. Crossing blades will either prompt you to mash the attack quickly to overpower your enemy or to lock into a brief minigame of alternating light and heavy attacks until you outmaneuver them and deliver a vicious blow; both moves are easy but look and feel badass thanks to the detailed physics and animations that send enemies staggering or leave them bisected anime-style, crown to jewels.
Capcom Capcom Capcom Capcom Capcom What this Onimusha does differently from every other game of its kind is embrace the physicality of the brawl. The way Musashi braces for an impact; the way he shifts to an overhead strike for a heavy attack that's easy for enemies to sidestep if you don't lead with a lighter horizontal swipe; the way walls and boards you can pry off the ground are an opportunity to deal quick and ruthless stagger damage. Way of the Sword toys with the idea of making these physics interactions its specialty, but it never really commits to them, with boss fights mostly falling back on more straightforward 'git gud' tests of patience and timing. It leaves a lot on the table for a sequel to build on, but even with their full potential unrealized the physics still make Musashi feel like he has a body . Literally built different, etc.
Strategic complexity comes mostly from the secondary weapons, Musashi's Oni Armaments; most of them play a key role, from peeling health or power souls off an enemy to smashing half their stamina meter in a single hit. It's so tempting to wait to use these until the perfect moment, but holding onto that meter just a little too long risks a boss getting in a clean hit and stealing the souls for themselves. It's a dance of patience and aggression that was still tripping me up when I had a boss down to the last 10% of their health, then suddenly lost my rhythm and was dead seconds later.
There's a fantastic clarity to all of the action: you could teach a Videogames 101 course using the boss attack patterns (tricky, but always learnable) in Way of the Sword, and the instant post-meter burn regret of popping too early. This is the kind of stuff Capcom's designers have excelled at for decades, just with a bit more emphasis on patience and timing than usual.
The panache and silliness of old Onimusha still comes through in much of the character design, too—just wait for the boss who's basically a demigod rockstar riffing on the Japanese high school delinquent trope, exaggerated pompadour and all.
Samurai spirit
I was pleased by how beautifully this action ran on my 9070 XT, often hitting 120 fps with all the settings turned up and AMD FSR4 set to quality. Other than brief hitches when loading or transitioning between cutscenes, performance is fantastic. And I think this is the best-looking RE Engine game Capcom's made when it comes to the facial animations, art direction and cutscenes—which makes it an extra shame that so much of the game takes place in a perpetually overcast, muddy Kyoto. Truly a baffling choice.
Izumo no Okuni (Image credit: Capcom) A shorter, more linear Onimusha with less time spent picking up boring junk would've truly been all killer no filler—but even with the filler, it's going to be a strong contender for the best combat of the year. But that's a box I really expected Capcom to check from the moment it brought Onimusha back to life.
More impressive is the lengths to which it goes to live up to Toshiro Mifune's resurrection. This series started with the fun but shallow premise of digitizing a famous actor as a samurai. Way of the Sword asks how to imbue that idea with purpose: What if the emotional core of the story revolved around Musashi's fabled journey from arrogant vagabond to a noble warrior? What if one of the other figures it plucked from history was the inventor of Kabuki, at this point a ferocious young girl who cares more about the people of Kyoto than Musashi does? What if the big bad, another famous Japanese warrior, was an absolute motherfucker ? This is the most fun I've had with a game's alternate history since Command & Conquer Red Alert's campy FMVs, and pushes the game up a tier from period action game to proper period piece. Bring on Way of the Two Swords with haste.

title: 「金铲铲之战」冲进iOS游戏畅销榜Top3！其五周年活动期间收入攀升的背后，藏着哪些手游开发者可复用的增长逻辑？
text:
8 月 30 日，腾讯旗下英雄联盟云顶之弈正版授权自走棋手游「金铲铲之战」五周年主活动开启。期间登录宝箱、连续领取奖励、赛季任务、限定装扮以及线下直播等多项内容也集中上线。
七麦数据监测显示，8 月 31 日 10 时，该游戏位列 App Store 游戏畅销榜 Top 3。这组榜单回答了一个关于游戏长线运营的关键问题： 一款成熟游戏产品如何将周年庆热度转化为玩家回流和付费转化。
占据游戏畅销榜头部席位，金铲铲五周年活动做对了什么？
五周年活动开启当日，该游戏相关话题登上抖音热榜。 七麦数据监测显示，8 月 31 日 10 时，该游戏位列 App Store 游戏畅销榜第 3，同时在游戏免费榜的排名也随之升高，位列榜单第 7。
「金铲铲之战」在iOS游戏畅销榜排名
对于已经运营五年的成熟游戏来说，这样的表现并不意外。周年庆的首要目标，是召回老玩家，引导他们重新上线对局、持续参与活动，最后才是道具、装扮类消费。两者结合来看，可以判断本次活动重心更偏向存量用户经营。
金铲铲五周年活动拆解：用系列动作实现用户唤回‑回访‑留存‑付费闭环
据悉，8 月 7 日「金铲铲之战」五周年庆典已正式启动，且当日起玩家完成每日对局首胜即可领取五周年棱彩兑换石福袋；8 月 20 日，该游戏推出了 “自然之力” 全新赛季，并同步上线了新弈子、新羁绊等；8 月 30 日集中上线了五周年宝箱、线上直播以及生日派对等内容。
这一系列动作的第一层意义是唤回老玩家。 借助周年情怀、社交话题、跨界合作与免费福利等，给了老玩家重新打开游戏的理由。
第二层是回访。 8 月 30 日‑9 月 1 日，玩家每日登录即可获得宝箱奖励；另外还有 7 日连续领取、每日首胜和对局任务等，把单次登录拆解为了多日的持续行为。
第三层是留存。 该游戏的 App Store 商店产品页面显示，1.14.34 版本在 8 月 19 日完成更新，并上线了“自然之力” 新赛季，带来 200 余种自然仙灵、十多种全新羁绊；8 月 27 日又做了版本平衡调整。保证玩家回归之后有全新内容可以体验，而不是领完奖励就离开。
第四层是付费转化。 在免费福利之外，活动还同步上线了限定装扮、竞技场召唤、折扣礼包等付费内容。免费福利与付费内容并行，在同一活动周期内覆盖了不同付费意愿的玩家。
综合下来可以看到，「金铲铲之战」通过一套完整的周年庆运营链路实现了用户唤回、回访、留存、付费转化的闭环。
金铲铲的这套打法并不是可以完全照搬的，对不同团队来说，想要真正要落到日常运营中，建议重点关注以下几个方面：
对游戏产品团队来说，优先关注回流用户占比、首胜任务完成率、7 日活动完成率。相比单日免费榜排名，这几项指标更能反映老用户是否回归并持续游戏。
对增长团队来说，需要把新赛季、周年回流、限定装扮拆分为不同的玩家人群。 可以借助 App Store 应用内活动来展示限时内容；借助商店自定产品页面来呈现不同的宣传侧重点，再通过 App Analytics 观察流量来源与转化效果，不要把全部流量统一给到同一套素材。
对商业化团队来说，榜单只能作为外部参考信号。真正需要复盘的是活动首购人数、付费用户规模、各价格档位转化情况，以及领取免费奖励的用户是否继续参与后续内容。只有这些数据，才能区分榜单高位是老用户惯性消费，还是周年活动带来的新增付费。
结语
结合该游戏本次的 App Store 榜单表现、官方活动排期以及 App 版本迭代节奏，我们可以看到： 「金铲铲之战」五周年更像是一次成熟游戏产品的存量用户经营，而非单纯冲新增下载的活动。 其中值得大家重点参考借鉴的，是该游戏的整套周年庆活动节奏。
你的游戏在推出周年活动时，是否已经把 “用户回归” 和 “用户留存” 拆成了两套独立指标？

title: 对话7年长青SLG制作人：市场未来会更卷，做出“不可替代”才有机会
text:
上线7年的《权力的游戏 凛冬将至》，依旧是 游族网络 的营收支柱之一。
近期游族网络公布2026上半年财报，财报显示今年上半年收入6.96亿元，归母净利润2.53亿元，实现营收净利双增。其中海外地区收入5.02亿元，同比增长13.16%，占比创下历史新高。
无论是此前的业绩预告还是此次的财报，都重点提到了《权力的游戏 凛冬将至》PC（以下简称权游），作为海外主力产品，持续贡献稳定流水，为业绩提供坚实支撑。
《权力的游戏 凛冬将至》
不久前 游戏日报 采访了《权游》制作人、游族网络 饭团工作室 负责人张志锋。张志锋告诉 游戏日报 《权游》自2019年在海外上线，近年来产品收入依旧稳中有升，张志锋将这样的成绩归结为三个原因：
一是权游IP本身具备的价值，对留存以及付费留存都有促进；
二是《权游》在所处的竞争环境，相比同类竞品有很大的品质优势；
三是产品版本节奏和克制度，七年来《权游》一直保持两周一个版本的更新频率，一直让玩家保持新鲜感，同时没有为了短期流水做商业化收割。
在聊到 SLG 出海机遇和挑战时，张志锋表示未来1-2年竞争烈度会达到峰值，真正能做成的团队除了拥有过硬的产品力外，一定是具备市场敏锐度，数据认知、雄厚的资金等必要条件。一年测试十数款产品是头部团队试错和迭代的常态节奏，在不断卷题材、碰机遇的环境下市场竞争会被推上新的高度。
张志锋还认为，未来有成熟底盘产品加上具备市场敏锐度的团队将有更多机会。
以下为采访实录。
游戏日报：游族的财报几乎每年都会提到《权游》，最近一年运营情况怎么样？它在游族内部是什么定位？
张志锋： 整体比较平稳，稳中有升。
定位上，游族有SLG和卡牌两条核心赛道，卡牌的支柱是《少年三国志》系列；SLG赛道目前的两个支柱分别是《权游》和《 Infinity Kingdom 》（战火与永恒）。
游戏日报：您认为《权游》从2019年上线到现在，保持长青的核心是什么？
张志锋： 第一是IP本身的价值，权游IP很强，对用户的留存、尤其是付费留存都有正面影响。我们后续也尝试过其他IP向的产品，确实IP向产品的长线会更好。
第二是用户基数。作为权游ip的底盘是中世纪品类。当ip核心用户买到一定程度后，中世纪题材的受众用户还可以作为更大的用户底盘。
第三是版本节奏和克制，七年来基本两个星期一个版本，让用户一直觉得有新东西。同时整体比较克制，没有为流水做大型商业化收割性的东西，持续补充养成维度，商业化定价稳定、一分钱一分货，让用户对商业化体系保持信任。
游戏日报：在做IP产品，尤其是有IP的SLG产品，由于SLG的重度属性，大家第一反应通常是“换皮”“骗氪”，《权游》是怎么做到七年多来一直让玩家喜欢的？
张志锋： 确实有很多IP产品的用户很难接受做成SLG，但权游IP的底色就是战争，跟SLG的匹配度非常高，小说本身也是基于中世纪战争架构的，所以用户觉得很合理。
我们在游戏里把整个沙盘还原了 维斯特洛大陆 ，北境是长城、君临城的位置等都比较考据，IP还原度做得很细致。玩家一起去攻打君临、龙家与狮家的战争、五王之乱的剧情，在IP上都合理，用户能接受。
当然也有用户因为觉得难玩、玩不太懂而流失，所以我们在入口侧下了功夫，尽量让用户觉得没那么难上手。上线初期免费送了很多IP向角色，后期用户对游戏的粘性高了再补充原创角色。运营过程中，用户慢慢从对IP的喜欢，转化到对整个社交游戏和玩法的喜爱。再往后更多是皮肤、外观这类炫耀性内容，没有一直数值逼氪，普通玩家也能玩。
游戏日报：《权游》是如何平衡“IP还原度”和“游戏可玩性”的？比如既满足IP粉丝诉求，又适配SLG玩家的玩法需求？
张志锋： 这个IP的价值更多在角色。我们底层把角色3D建模做得精度很高，用了PBR工艺，每个指挥官都经过演员本人监修，还原度高、品质精良，用户会觉得这是一个正版授权、品质很高的大型游戏，信任度很高。
玩法上，因为IP底色偏战争，转化很容易。比如想做同盟对战，想做全服抵抗的异鬼入侵，脑子一转就能想到，不需要深度挖掘。换一个别的IP可能就不行，比如把一部宫斗剧题材做成SLG很难，但这个 IP 的世界观天然适配，所以过程中其实没有权衡，想做就套上去了。
美术还原上，我们用很低的性能消耗在沙盘上把君临城、凛冬城这些做出来，视觉冲击很强，玩家想打下君临城、自己占下君临城的意愿很强。我们原有的十几个城基本都能找到对应的城市，坐标都能还原到位。
唯一的难点是传统SLG从外圈往里打，而我们的地图是整块维斯特洛大陆，只能为此妥协，没有完全从外往里打，但整体的可玩性没有变化。
游戏日报：游族近年把中台运营并入项目组，您说过研运一体让团队搭了自己的发行线，对买量回收认知更强了，整体收益大于成本增加。能不能举一个“发行数据倒逼研发调整设计”的具体例子？
张志锋： 进入AI时代之后，这种研运打通的趋势更明显。我以前做研发，其实不关注发行，现在从买量成本就开始关注：哪些素材留存更好、哪些素材成本更低。
了解之后，产品侧会做调整，比如发现某类素材成本一直很低，就把相关的东西提炼出来做进游戏里，去承接这些低成本素材，跑出高消耗、高留存。
现在研发也会参加素材会，甚至有些跑得好的素材是研发自己用AI设计制作的视频或图片。研发和发行现在基本不分工了，发行也会深入玩游戏找问题，研发和发行坐在一起，是一条链路，互相打通。
游戏日报：饭团工作室最核心的研发标签和差异化优势是什么？
张志锋： 首先是人才，我们拥有一支长期磨合、稳定的核心团队，成员之间合作都已超过十年，每个人对用户的理解都比较深入，话题很容易聊到一起去，关键问题能很快形成小组去解决。
其次是海外长线运营的经验。我们清楚怎么跟用户相处、怎么搭客服体系、关注哪些运营指标。每个月付费用户流失出现异常时，客服会快速介入，再从产品角度解决。我们有一套长线的思维框架，只要跑起来了，后面问题不大。
还有技术框架的底子，不用从头反复搭建。现在更多是在找SLG+X的入口，新框架出来之后，能更快迭代新产品，以个把月为维度去迭代、找新的入口，做出能跑出量的产品。
游戏日报：饭团工作室是国内较早深耕全球SLG出海的团队之一，当前SLG出海的竞争维度都有哪些变化？
张志锋： 首先是竞争烈度非常大，市场集中度持续提升。第二是海量厂商在做各种各样的尝试，出手速度极快，用户被反复触达得有些疲乏，核心用户又被头部产品带走。综合来看现在整体难度我认为是相当高的。
游戏日报：您如何看待2026年和未来SLG出海的机遇与挑战？团队是否会调整出海布局策略？
张志锋： 我觉得2026年和2027年的竞争烈度会达到峰值。
真正能做成的团队除了拥有过硬的产品力外，一定是具备市场敏锐度，数据认知、雄厚的资金等必要条件。
现在开发速度会越来越快，AI的发展和在已有框架下只迭代X，所以接下来更多是卷题材、碰机遇的空间。当前市场客观因素可能会有一部分新的窗口期。
对我们来说，核心SLG的沉淀都在这里，我们还会坚持做，但会在X的部分考虑自己的特点。核心就是保持在场，持续迭代，等待窗口期。
游戏日报：SLG+X轻量化类型的游戏近几年趋势很明显，您认为出现这样趋势的原因是什么？
张志锋： 最直接的原因是头部吸引。头部X+SLG的产品收入太高，吸引了很多厂商入局。X+SLG比传统SLG有更大的规模，头部产品比传统SLG更快和更高的达到流水的峰值，用便宜的成本获取用户，又能拥有SLG的长线收入模型。
但是接下来难度还是提升了，因为一堆的产品在做X，广告系统识别也越来越智能，不一定能用便宜的成本获取用户。接下来更多是怎么跟头部打出你的明确竞争力，X这部分要探索出自己的特点，打出自己竞争力的逻辑，让你这个东西变成市场上没办法替代的东西。
游戏日报：没办法替代，怎么理解？
张志锋： 核心是让产品在市场上具备不可替代性，用户想玩某个题材、获得某种体验，市场上找不到其他产品。
在同质化非常高的SLG市场里，找到自己游戏带给用户独特体验的切入点。在用户心智上有一个独属的标签。
因为同质化高，用户很多已经被其它SLG洗过，如果用户无法找到必须玩你的这块游戏的理由，他的流失几率会大大提升。所以要在垂类里找到自己无可替代的部分，这是差异化的关键。让用户一想到这类体验，就联想到你的产品。
但是这个差异化又不能太偏太创新，太偏的话，体量做不大，太创新的话难把控。所以这里是个难点。
游戏日报：是否可以把这种思路理解为向更细分的领域挖掘？
张志锋： 是的，举个例子：黑帮题材。黑帮也卷过很多产品，但市场上出了一个监狱题材，监狱就是黑帮题材里能打出来的那个细分点，你想玩黑帮但玩不到监狱，而监狱就有自己的核心用户群。
游戏日报：未来在SLG+X领域，什么样的产品会有更多机会？
张志锋： 我个人的看法，首先要有成熟的底盘，这是必要条件，否则前期再吸引人，后期底盘不扎实也难以持久。但这一判断不完全准确，因为用户群体不同，对底盘的诉求也不同，所以要针对X调整底盘，这里没有标准答案，但团队要有调底盘的能力。
第二，最终都回到人的能力上，X的能力更多来自发行的市场敏锐度。优势会出现在投放大量产品、进行海量投放的公司身上：它们持续投放，能敏锐捕捉市场用户的变化和风向，更容易命中。
第三，是AI。AI时代最大的变化是开发迭代速度的跃升，过去调整一个玩法可能需要数周，现在在已有框架下迭代X，周期大幅缩短。团队如果能善用AI工具辅助研发决策、素材制作和数据分析，就能以更低成本做更多尝试，在市场窗口期内快速试错和定版。接下来拼的不只是创意，更是从创意到上线的转化速度，AI正在提升创意落地的效率。
游戏日报：如果要给一些想入局SLG赛道的新团队建议或忠告，你会说什么？
张志锋： 对新的研发团队来说，我认为要谨慎。因为可以把产品做出来，但要走到最后，一个强大的发行团队更为重要。

title: 拿命换流量！死亡游戏ADV《BUZZ or DIE》年内发售！
text:
爆火便可免罪，落败即为死刑
讲谈社创作者实验室宣布，独立游戏创作者凡（@EgoMixer）正式加入「讲谈社Game Creators' Lab（GCL）」成为实验室成员。与此同时，正在开发中的冒险游戏《BUZZ or DIE》Steam商店页面于今日改版，并公开了全新主视觉图。
是活下去，还是沦落为全民的玩物，决定这一切的，只有观众的「点赞」——。本作是一款以一档由各有隐情的死刑犯出演的综艺节目为舞台的冒险游戏。玩家将与搭档组成二人小队，揭开对手不为人知的过去，并将这些经历作为素材，制作短视频和封面图，争取更多曝光量。最终获胜者不仅能够获得无罪释放，还将得到「实现任何愿望」的权利；而失败者将要面对的，则不仅是在直播中被公开处刑……还会沦为奴隶用仿生机器人的原型，被无止境地践踏尊严。
游戏主要分为两个部分。在「调查部分」中，玩家将阅读囚犯之间的对话与回忆，逐步挖掘对手的过去；而在「封面图制作部分」中，则需要利用调查获得的素材，根据短视频的主题组合合适的图片与关键词，制作出一张封面图。打造足够吸睛、能够赚取更多播放量的封面图，引领自己走向胜利吧。
本作角色插画由漫画家冈田淳司老师担任。凡所打造的黑暗流行世界观，与冈田淳司老师笔下精美且极具独特审美趣味的插画风格相互碰撞，敬请期待两位带来的独特化学反应。
在这场被流量支配的死亡真人秀中挣扎胜出后，你最终能否抵达救赎的彼岸？《BUZZ or DIE》预计于2026年内正式发售。
※本作包含部分暴力、血腥表现，以及可能引起精神不适的内容。
商店页面：https://store.steampowered.com/app/2899240/BUZZ_or_DIE/
PV：https://youtu.be/wzOZRIsQpy0
■不火就只有死路一条。拿对手的过去当素材，拼命赚取「点赞」吧
与玩家一同参加这场赌上生死的游戏的，是新兴宗教前教主——鹭岛
玩家将被安排与一名死刑犯搭档组成二人小队，参加这档以性命为赌注的综艺节目「BUZZ or DIE」。
决定「BUZZ or DIE」胜负的，是观众的投票。想要获胜，手段只有一个——制作以对手为素材的短视频，获得比对方更多的「点赞」。在进入对手精神世界、挖掘其过去的「调查部分」中抓住对方的弱点，再制作出能够吸引观众眼球的抢眼封面图吧。无论使用什么手段，只要没能爆火，等待你的就只有死亡。
把对手悲惨的过去变成供人取乐的节目素材吧！
根据封面图制作方案的不同，搭档制作的短视频内容也会发生变化。
■参赛者全都是死刑犯。角色插画由漫画家冈田淳司老师担任
死刑犯之间针锋相对的互呛，以及落败角色狼狈不堪的模样，也同样值得关注
搞笑艺人出身的爆炸犯与天才黑客少女、革命者与食人厨师——等等。聚集在节目中的，全部都是犯下重罪、两人一组的死刑犯。每一对搭档之间都存在着不浅的因缘，而随着节目的推进，他们之间的关系也将逐渐浮出水面。
角色立绘及剧情事件CG均由漫画家冈田淳司老师（代表作：『双生遊戯』『タタキザサイドハッスル』）全新绘制，敬请期待。
【创作者简介】
凡 （X: https://x.com/EgoMixer）
擅长塑造个性鲜明、独具特色的角色，以及构建黑暗、富有解读空间的世界观。
过往作品包括《EgoMixer》《一路十二时》等。
【游戏信息】
游戏名称：BUZZ or DIE
支持平台：Steam
Steam商店页面：https://store.steampowered.com/app/2899240/BUZZ_or_DIE/
预计支持语言：日语、英语、简体中文
游戏类型：冒险游戏
预计发售时间：2026年内
售价：未定
游玩人数：1人
开发者：凡（X：https://x.com/EgoMixer）
发行商：株式会社讲谈社
版权标识：©︎凡／讲谈社
■关于讲谈社创作者实验室（https://creatorslab.kodansha.co.jp/）
株式会社讲谈社第四事业本部于2021年6月成立的研发部门。
该部门以“重新定义编辑”为理念，与各领域创作者建立广泛连接，不局限于书籍与杂志的形式，持续向社会推出多种多样的内容作品。
旗下包括：
・企划独立游戏创作者扶持及新作开发的「讲谈社游戏实验室」
・运营匹配型漫画投稿平台DAYS NEO等服务的「UGC媒体实验室」
